title: Cassette, London WC2: ‘One of the greatest dishes I’ve eaten all year’ – restaurant review | Grace Dent on restaurants
summary:
A discombobulating brew of the seemingly casual with the deadly bloody serious

I booked my lunch table at Cassette, a new French restaurant in Covent Garden, central London, while watching a viral video of a blasé Parisian couple, mid-riot, sipping wine and smoking Gauloises near the Arc de Triomphe. Yes, fiery flames of mass anarchy, but also, yes, finishing one’s glass is important, too. The Brits keep opening Parisian-style restaurants as a quiet admission that these people are really bloody cool, and this new one from Mark Gurney and Matt Bushnell, the pair behind Peckham’s Levan (also very cool, incidentally), serves the likes of a coq au vin jaune pie with a chicken leg saluting from its crust, and panisse with chopped mussels and green tomato. There’s also pork chop with sauce Talleyrand, Maldon oysters with beurre blanc, and a cocktail called Jet Fuel that combines Get 27, the green mint liqueur that gives every Parisian a starry-eyed memory of their parents’ dinner parties, with calvados and coffee liqueur.

Cassette is a discombobulating brew of the seemingly casual with the actually deadly bloody serious. Yes, dress up fancy, if you wish, but you can also slide in here in jeans and knitwear for a casual midweek vol-au-vent. No one will judge you. Service will at first come at you brasserie-style – casual, no stress – but can very quickly turn nerdy, obsessive and wallowing in ingredients, provenance and technique. If you want to geek out over bleu d’Auvergne or the consistency of the mascarpone cream, the staff will indulge you. The wine list starts at a kindly £29 a bottle, but soon climbs up into nosebleed territory via grower champagnes from the likes of Jérôme Prévost, a 2014 Jura savagnin, a detour to the volcanic Italian island of Pantelleria and a £350 Valentini trebbiano. In other words, Cassette is a clandestine foodie paradise.

The loos are nightclubby, tiled and, frankly, a bit down at heel, and the decor is pretty functional, clean and tidy, but the trump card right now is chef Essa Fakhry. In kitchen terms, Fakhry is Dublin-reared, having run the stoves at 777, a riotous contemporary Mexican and tequila joint, before going on to open Note in 2021, a wine bar that soon turned up on every “go there bloody quick” list and then slid into the Michelin Guide. After that, he put in an appearance at Planque, everyone’s favourite wine fiend’s paradise in Haggerston, east London. Humanness is captured in every pore and wrinkle of all nine of Jan van Eyck’s portraits, united for the first time by the National Gallery. The paintings have been loaned from Berlin, Vienna, Dresden, Bruges and Sibiu in Romania, in a triumph of cultural exchange that proves the blockbuster show is still very much alive. And so, it almost seems, are the people depicted in it, who appear so real we might “recognise them on the tube”, as the exhibition’s co-curator Nicholas Flory put it, even given their extravagant headgear.

A purplish wart, a tiny scar, bloodshot eyes, sagging jowls and dirty fingernails – it is the intimate details of Van Eyck’s likenesses that transformed Renaissance portraiture and make his sitters so relatable, in modern parlance, today. Like a novelist, the artist wanted to create the impression of capturing his subjects in a moment in time.

A Russian cargo ship was hit by a Ukrainian drone and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, as Finland’s prime minister said Kyiv had the right to hit back against its “aggressor”. The Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, suggested the incident in the Gulf of Finland had to do with Russia’s war in Ukraine. “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Orpo said on X. “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”

Hours later, a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace, according to the Finnish defence minister, who drew a possible link between the two incidents. “The suspected airspace violation may be linked to rescue or monitoring operations involving a cargo ship that was damaged in the Gulf of Finland,” Antti Hakkanen said on X.

Petteri Blomvall, an officer at the Finnish Border Guard, said: “I can confirm that a Ukrainian drone strike hit the ship in the morning that caused the fire … The crew from the ship has been evacuated, the ship is anchored and the firefighting is ongoing.”

The Finnish Defence Forces identified the ship as the Sparta II, which is under Ukrainian and US sanctions, according to the site Opensanctions. The website said the ship was suspected of transporting weapons from Syria to Russia. The MarineTraffic maritime monitoring website said the Sparta II had departed St Petersburg around 11pm and was bound for the port of Baltiysk, in the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

Finland’s defence ministry said it had immediately informed Nato of the drone strike. It also said temporary restrictions were being enforced in the airspace and maritime area of the eastern part of the Gulf. Rattled by Russia’s invasion, Finland joined Nato in 2023, dropping decades of military non-alignment. The Gulf of Finland is a key maritime passage for Russia, leading to the former capital St Petersburg.

It is undoubtedly the best of his projects to date, and is sure to be one of the year’s breakouts, if recent successes by sharp-tongued songwriters such as Cameron Winter and This Is Lorelei are anything to go by. Emperors took a final sigh and slipped under the table, ministers burst while tucking into their dessert, poets quietly starved to death or choked on their own self-importance. Vienna’s cuisine has outlasted them all: a little bit too heavy, a bit too greasy, and always covered in breadcrumbs or sprinkles.

Consider the schnitzel, for example. The Wiener Schnitzel is a legend, supposedly a dish of world-class stature: golden-yellow and wavy, spilling over the plate, with a delicate wedge of lemon daintily nestled beside it (in some of the more upmarket establishments, it even comes wrapped in a little linen pouch). There are few dishes that are so passionately raved about while being so fervently disparaged. The schnitzel has to be pounded until paper-thin, the breadcrumb coating must be light and airy, the accompanying potato salad prepared with a marinade of beef stock, vinegar, oil and finely chopped onions – without (without!) mayonnaise. Anything else is an affront. In Vienna you can get heated debates with strangers about all sorts of ideological nonsense. But the quality of a schnitzel is not up for discussion. The Viennese take food seriously, but without coming across as particularly serious. If you’ve nothing to laugh about at the dinner table, you’ve nothing to laugh about in life.
